text: The Genesis Melody
A Quick Foreword
Hey.
Hi.
Before we get started, I wanted to let you know that I love you.
Yes, that’s extremely awkward to say in our generation, but it really shouldn’t be.
Of course, I don’t know you, and we’ve never met.
So my love for you is a bit limited, but you are an Image of God like me, so…
I love you.
Oops, I said it again.
My goal here is to help you see a pattern in Scripture that I think should be important to your life.
We’re going to look mainly at Genesis 1-23.
In these chapters God works with his human partners in many ways, but the structure of the text is very carefully designed.
God creates and calls, those parts will be fun to study, but he also tests and brings about collapse in response to human partners.
Trying to understand how God is at work even through a collapse should help give you hope and confidence in things yet to come, so those parts should not to be overlooked.
This pattern has been woven into all scripture, and the more you study, the more you will see.
Let’s become apprentices together so that we can know|love Him more.
Introduction and Motivation
This guide is organized into three main sections:
Introduction and Motivation
The part you are about to read.
Melody Observations
A detailed look at Genesis 1-22, broken into three parts:
Genesis 1-7: The Template of the Melody
Genesis 8-11: The Second Round of the Melody
Genesis 11:27-22:19: Cycles Three to Seven with Avraham
From there, this guide will pivot when we read the details of the seventh cycle's collapse and re-creation moments.
We’ll let the story guide us, but something will happen naturally when we read about Avraham's test and the oath that Yahweh makes.
The Melody Points to Jesus
When you read the Bible, it’s tempting to read only the parts about Jesus and the early church.
However, God’s grand song is best experienced when the Old Testament paves the way.
This guide is the same.
You should expect to enjoy the final section about Jesus the most, but do try to read the earlier sections first.
Think of it like a movie, the climax means more when you haven't skipped the first hour.
Summary: What is The Genesis Melody?
When you approach the Bible, what do you see there?
Well, what do you expect to see there?
Over time we have been trained to see only some parts of the Bible.
Our expectations are often at odds with our ability to simply receive the message.
This guide will focus on reading Genesis 1-23 trying to see patterns.
The goal is to approach the text as a blank slate.
To be honest, I’m not capable of doing that either, but it’s important to know the mindset we’d like to have.
Shaping the Bible to meet our expectations is rather pointless.
The goal is to open ourselves up, so that we can be shaped by the Bible.
I’m really excited to share with you some things I've gotten to see in Genesis.
Through this writing process, I’ve felt the guiding presence of the Spirit myself and I’m just amazed at what these authors have been able to create.
The Hebrew Bible, the Old Testament, was carefully written by humans partnering with the work of the Spirit over the course of hundreds of years to make God known to us.
As a result, it is a VERY dense, beautiful collection of ancient scrolls with many layers to unpack.
Readers who start at the beginning, myself included, see only a small fraction of the depth the authors are communicating.
However, the goal of this guide is not to learn everything.
We’ll choose to focus on just one significant layer that is often overlooked.
There is a clear, repeated creation melody that runs throughout the Hebrew Bible and into the New Testament.
Once you have eyes to see and ears to hear how the authors replay the notes, you won’t be able to miss them as you continue to read the Bible.
This song starts with God bringing about creation, life, and blessing.
He then calls human partners to share in the work.
Often characteristic human choices lead to the division of relationships causing things to come to a head in a collapse.
At other times, pattern breakers step in who choose to trust and obey God.
Strangely, the collapse often falls on them just the same, but they go through the collapse with God.

Much like the rain, which falls on the just and the unjust alike, they too experience genuine suffering, but through them God can once again bring about creation, life, and blessing from the non-life.
Understanding how God continually brings about and sustains life is foundational not just in the Bible, but in our own lives as well.
So the authors of the Bible provide a decoder ring, beginning on page one, to unlock the rest of the story.
Before we get started, I should explain the title.
The word genesis means two things to us: first, it refers to the scroll of Genesis, but it also simply means what the word means.
The word genesis comes from the Greek γένεσις (génesis), meaning "origin, source, beginning, or birth”.
Matthew liked this word and so do I.
So when choosing a title for a repeated creation pattern, a genesis, that is easily seen in the scroll of Genesis, it seemed only fitting to call it The Genesis Melody.
However, don’t be fooled!
The author of life keeps creating well beyond the pages of Genesis.
Background
The melody is discussed at length in the BibleProject Genesis Classroom series, namely, these five courses:
Heaven and Earth
Adam to Noah
Noah to Abraham
Abraham
Jacob

From these courses the most succinct summaries of what Tim Mackie calls “The Melody” are found in session 11 of the Abraham class, titled The Genesis 1-11 Melody Repeats, or sessions 2 and 3 of the Jacob class, The Thematic Melody of Genesis 1-9 and Abraham Replays the Melody.
However, if you are new to the melody concept, it’s best to start from the beginning.
Through his studies, Tim began to see how the authors replayed similar concepts, often in the same order, that felt like the melody of a song.
It emerged after years of teaching, exploring commentaries, and discussing the text with reading communities.

These concepts have become so important to Tim that he starts nearly every course with a recap of The Melody, see the Joseph class, The Thematic Melody of the Hebrew Bible, or the Ezekiel class, The Main Themes of the Torah.
It leads Tim to make statements like:
“And that is a way to summarize almost all the narrative cycles of the Hebrew Bible.
It's these stories of God giving a blessing.
And it's great until they're faced with a choice that the blessing puts in front of them, whether they'll trust or not.
Just a zillion times over in all of these stories and poems.
Yes, trusting what God said, even when my circumstances look like the opposite of what God said.
And what if, when my circumstances look like the opposite of what God said, what if I'm in the test?
He sees the bible as a song that gets more complex as the patterns repeat.
Here is a rather extended quote from Tim and Jon for why they call it a melody:
“Think of the use of melody in music.
You can hear an unmistakable progression of notes that form a coherent whole.
However, in sophisticated music such as orchestral music, that melody will develop with harmonies and innovations.
However, no matter how much innovation in the melody, the heart of the melody is still present.
As you listen, the melody gets more interesting, more nuanced, and more beautiful.
This is the same way biblical literature works.
The Bible introduces us to a core set of narrative beats that repeat across the whole Bible, each time with variations but always recognizable as the same pattern.
Genesis 1-11 establishes the musical notes.
The rest of the Hebrew Bible plays those notes in an escalating series of variations, never identically, always recognizably.
The melody of the Bible is building towards something.
The melody escalates toward a climactic moment in the life, death and resurrection of Jesus and in the people who follow him.
This guide builds on those insights, to lay out the melody for you and help us all meditate on the purpose.
What were these authors communicating by intentionally structuring the text in this way?
Why Study the Melody
What is the value in seeing the structure of the melody?
The main focus in the Genesis courses is how the repeated notes should be ringing in our ears to link parts of the melody.
Parallel stories might be separated by many chapters, but with only a few distinct notes the authors can put them side-by-side in your mind.
One story informs the other, and both benefit from the connection.
Let’s take a short but deep dive to consider one specific example: Genesis 3:6-7a.
You probably know this text well.
Notice the key words as you read it again.
3:6 and the woman saw that the tree was good for eating,
and that it was desirable to the eyes,
and that the tree was desirable to make one wise,
and she took from its fruit and she ate;
and she gave also to her husband with her, and he ate.
7 and the eyes of both of them were opened,
The best way to hear what the authors are communicating in this passage is not to focus on these words alone.
In isolation, these words have some value, but to fully grasp the verse, you have to spend time thinking about how it connects to the greater narrative.
As we will soon discuss, this verse is a choice in the first round of the melody.
Let's compare it to the choice in melody four, Genesis 16:2-4, by reading the story of Sarai, Avram, and Hagar.
Note, Avram is just an alternative spelling of Abram, who will later be renamed Abraham.
In the BibleProject translation, you will see a few surprising spellings to help us more faithfully pronounce the original Hebrew names.
Additionally, Yahweh, God's personal name, is used when appropriate instead of translating it to God or LORD.
If that makes you feel uncomfortable, just replace “Yahweh” with “God” as you read (that's fine).
Notice the repeated words here that echo the Eden passage above.
16:2 And Sarai said to Avram, “Look, please!
Yahweh has restrained me from giving birth.
Please, go into my slave-girl.
Perhaps I can be built up by means of her.”
And Avram listened to the voice of Sarai.
3 And Sarai, the wife of Avram took Hagar, her Egyptian slave-girl, at the end of ten years of Avram dwelling in the land of Canaan, and she gave her to Avram, her husband, as a wife.
4 And he went into Hagar and she became pregnant, and she saw that she was pregnant, and her mistress became cursed in her eyes.
The reuse pattern goes from taking a piece of fruit to taking an image of God.
That escalated quickly!
These two choices are separated by 13 chapters, but they are clear hyperlinks.
If you set them alongside one another, you can see how they are similar and how they are different.
Additionally, they are both inversions of an earlier choice pattern from Genesis 2:18-22, where God himself sees what is not good, then takes, builds, and gives.
God models correct behavior for us before we face our test.
There’s something to think about there.
Let’s read that story and consider how all three passages inform one another.
2:18 and Yahweh God said,
"It is not good for the human to be alone
I will make a help-counterpart for him

21 and Yahweh caused to fall a deep sleep on the human and he slept and he took one from his sides and he closed the flesh of its place 22 and Yahweh built the side which he took from the human into woman, and he brought her to the human
The authors signal connections through both word repetition and shared symbols.
They are clues to help us become better readers.
They seem subtle at first, but with effort, it’s remarkable the depth of understanding your group can reach as you hold repeated stories in your mind.
God saw good, tov, טוב, in Genesis 1 seven times, ending in a “very good.”

Humans, however, characteristically see what is good for themselves in their own eyes: we take and eat (an image to consume in this case), then give (send out non-life choices), as shown in 3:6 and 16:3.
But God sees what is not good, something in our world that is broken: He takes and builds (multiplies abundance), then gives (sends out life).
Both the similarities and the differences pop out as significant when you compare rounds of the melody.
Finally, in both human replays, the male character is said to have “listened to the voice of his wife,” instead of trusting God.
Who will you trust to receive the knowledge of good and bad?
Structure
There are many notes in the melody as it develops, changes, and repeats, but we’ll focus on only the most fundamental four notes: Creation, Calling (Identity), Testing and Choices, and Collapse.
The cycle goes around like a circle.
For the purposes of this guide, we will consider how this four-part melody is repeated seven times from Genesis 1 to 22.

To be clear, the repeated pattern can be broken down in many ways and variations are welcome as we all understand the Biblical authors slightly differently, but the four most central notes of the melody seem to be:
Creation
The transition from a state of non-life, chaos, situations-that-don’t-work into a state of life, order, and blessing.
The gift of life and blessing to multiply.
The process starts with the smallest presence of God as ruakh, the Holy Spirit, or the Word of God.
Calling / Naming / Identification
God chooses to work with partners!
These chosen humans are named, identified, or called to accomplish work in God’s rescue story.
An anointed one or group of chosen people are identified and sent for a purpose.
Rise up!
Testing and Choices
This phase reveals the heart of the human partners.
Will they trust God and build life or see what is good in their own eyes to consume.
Collapse
Theoretically speaking, the melody should not require a collapse.
Partners with God could always pass the test and use agreed upon healthy rhythms of reset like Sabbath cycles and Jubilee to avoid a collapse.
However, practically speaking there is always a collapse.
Choices that simply don’t work pile up to a breaking point.
Sometimes humans are the spark.
At other times, God initiates the collapse to wash away, but always for the purpose of future restoration.
The forest has a fire, the trees suffer, and God chooses not to stop the fire, but to work with partners through it.
These can be cosmic in scope, like the 10 plagues, the fall of Jerusalem, Exile, or the Flood, or personal, like Hagar, Ruth and Naomi, Stephen, or Jonah.
But in every case, the important part is what happens next.
God’s modus operandi is not a difficult pattern to spot.
Even so, there are two perspectives to hold in tension.
One asks, “Why would you fear something that God is fully in control of?”
The other would say, “How can God allow his people to suffer?”
Both are valid, and Scripture makes room for both, simultaneously trusting God while still crying out.
The longest phase of the melody is often Testing and Choices which can be many rounds of accumulating choices over generations.
However, in some chapters it will be just a single really poor choice.
Revealing the heart usually takes time and second chances are frequent.
It is supposed to be an opportunity for growth as it happens, but depending on how human partners respond to their calling and make choices the cycle can follow one of two paths.
The two paths are mentioned through the Bible, for example Matthew 7:13-14: “For wide is the gate and broad is the road that leads to destruction, and many enter through it.
But small is the gate and narrow the road that leads to life, and only a few find it.”
In this guide, we’ll call these paths: characteristic human choices or pattern breakers choices.
On the broad path there is no sense of receiving a calling, the calling is still there, but it is not received, so can be omitted.
Then the choices focus on conceiving for yourself what is good.
This leads to the division of relationships, and necessitates a pending collapse.
However, God still works through the collapse.
The notes for the ‘characteristic human’ pattern are actually easier to spot in Genesis 1 to 22, as there are more humans making those choices.
We will hear those notes again and again, so we will track those as the main pattern, but that doesn’t describe everyone.
Pattern Breakers!
Now, you might be thinking that this melody seems pretty gloom-and-doom.
Everything ends in collapse!
Is life really an inevitable downward spiral that ends in a collapse?
That’s depressing!
No, of course not.
That is the characteristic human pattern, NOT the way to life.
I think these authors love to make patterns just to break them.
Let’s look at Genesis 5 for a moment which uses a very clear pattern.
The text below is super long, but I bet you can see the point I'm making about pattern breaking in two seconds.
15 And Mahalalel lived sixty-five years,
and he caused the birth of Jared.
16 And Mahalalel lived eight hundred and thirty years after he became the father of Jared,
and he caused the birth of sons and daughters.
17 And all the days of Mahalalel were eight hundred and ninety-five years,
and he died.
18 And Yared lived one hundred and sixty-two years,
and he caused the birth of Enoch.
19 And Yared lived eight hundred years after he became the father of Enoch,
and he caused the birth of sons and daughters.
20 And all the days of Yared were nine hundred and sixty-two years,
and he died.
21 And Enoch lived sixty-five years,
and he caused the birth of Methuselah,
22 and Enoch walked with God three hundred years after he became the father of Methuselah,
and he caused the birth of sons and daughters,
23 and all the days of Enoch were three hundred and sixty-five years,
24 and Enoch walked with God; and he was not, for God took him.
The point is NOT the pattern.
The point is the pattern breaker!
As we listen for the notes in the melody, be especially on the lookout for pattern breaker moments.
Indeed, God is able to work through characteristic human choices, but see what God can do with the pattern breakers.
These choices lead to life.
The partners who break the characteristic pattern do not avoid the collapse, but rather they receive their calling and go through the collapse with God.
To be clear, it is the characteristic human choices that necessitate the collapse, but this group equally experiences the collapse.
In fact, sometimes pattern breakers experience more suffering in this age.
In response to that truth, it seems to me like God had two choices: take away free will or join us.
However, for some reason we don't deserve, God loves us, so He only had one choice…
Join us!
Perhaps, the circle here would look more like this.
What is impossible for man is possible with God, to go through a collapse.
Pattern breakers listen to God's voice, then get an opportunity to become partners in creation as God renews life not just in Genesis 1-23, but throughout the Bible.
But I’m getting ahead of myself.
First, we need to make sure we're receiving the Word of God faithfully and representing the source of truth accurately.

For example, this simple binary model of “some people are bad (characteristic human choices), some people are good (pattern breakers)” almost makes it seem like the pattern breakers have earned salvation.
However, when you dive into the details of this text and see the complexity of humans, you will come to realize that God's mercy is the driving factor in genesis, not humans.
For example, in the fourth collapse it's solely God's chosen partners Avram and Sarai that cause the collapse, and God responds by blessing and renaming Avraham!
God's radical love results in undeserved mercy which is unexpected and wonderful.
Perhaps the circle that best captures most of Avraham’s life leading up to the seventh cycle is:
When your deserve meter hits zero either individually or communally, cry out for mercy.
There are no works by which you can save your own life anyway.
Fortunately, in the melody, there are indeed times when God pulls someone kicking and screaming through the fire and into new life.
Interestingly, though, long term that won't work for people either, there is a necessary partnership in maintaining life.
OK enough guesswork on extracting themes, let's actually start doing Bible study to see if any of this is consistent with the true message God has given us.
Melody Observations
This middle section is the most academic, but also the heart of this guide.
If you are a person who spends time in biblical scholarship, to you I say “Enjoy!”
However, if you are a normal person without a rich background in Bible study, then to you I say “You can do it!”
Try to be like the people Paul met in Berea in Acts 17:11, “They received the message with great eagerness and examined the Scriptures every day to see if what Paul said was true.”
Genesis 1-7: The Melody Template
Instead of abstractly describing the characteristics of the notes, let’s look at the template of The Genesis Melody provided in Genesis 1-7.
These early chapters of Genesis are intentionally placed at the start of this massive collection as an introduction to the entire work.
They will plant seeds for themes that will take volumes to unpack.
If we allow them to properly shape our imagination and world view, we will become better Bible readers.
Through prayer, meditation, study, and time the biblical authors have shared God's message with us, but work is also necessary to receive it today.
How would Jesus have expressed this point?
In John 4:37-38 Jesus quotes an unusual phrase: “Thus the saying ‘One sows and another reaps’ is true...
Others have done the hard work, and you have reaped the benefits of their labor.”
Parables can have more than one meaning, a common Hebrew Bible technique, but, for our theme study, the seed sown represents the Wisdom of God planted in His Word.
These authors have worked with the Spirit to plant the key insights, but communication requires work from both the speaker and the listener.
We have to put in time together with the Spirit to convert words into a relationship, so that we can live in a right relationship with Him.
The authors use analogies that we can understand, like seed or light, but it all centers around taking on God's view of reality as truth.
The only way to reap this freely given fruit is by meditating on it over time, then living it out in our lives.
Let's get started by looking for the melody in Genesis 1-7 using the table below.
As you read the text, note that the name Elohim is yet another name for God, a bit less personal than Yahweh.
Again, feel free to translate “Elohim” as “God” if it makes you feel more comfortable.
Also, Ruakh is a Hebrew word which means Spirit, wind, or breath, more on that later.
Melody Cycle 1 Creation
Genesis 1:1 - 2:3 plus 2:4-15
After the seven-word Hebrew title of Genesis 1:1, we read about the precreation state of watery chaos, a standard image for nothing at that point in history.
However, with the presence of Elohim about to act, hovering as Ruakh over the face of the waters, we have hope.
Elohim speaks to create light and divides those chaos waters to bring order to the sea, sky, and land in Days 1-3.
He then fills those spaces with inhabitants in Days 4-6, starting with the lights in the sky, which are called signs.
He makes living beings to fill those spaces, giving them a blessing to be fruitful and multiply.
Ultimately, God creates the human in His image, male and female He created them, which He sees as “very good.”
Finally, on the 7th day, God rests, i.e., takes up residence and rules without conflict.
In the imagination of the Ancient Near East, when a ruler rests, it is a time of shalom, peace within the land.
We know this story well, thinking of it as a one-time creation event, but we need to keep reading to realize that creation is a cycle.
It will repeat!
Still in the Creation section, Genesis 2:4-6 offers another perspective of non-life, a barren desert without water.
God brings about life first via a stream, then the human, and finally trees, all in fun Hebrew wordplay.
Again, God’s life is present, gently breathing the breath of life into the human.
Melody Cycle 1 Calling
Genesis 1:27 and 2:15
The calling in the first round of the melody is the most significant in the Bible.
Every human is called an Image of God, the Imago Dei in Latin.
That identification is used as a present tense, you are right now an Image of God, but that’s a surprising phrase.
It is the true identity of every human, but I don’t personally feel like we’ve fully received that calling yet.
It reminds me of Ephesians 2:6, where Paul says that God has already “raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus”.
It is a calling that is true, but I think God sees me differently than I see myself.
The text then goes on to call us rulers over the entire cosmos that God has created.
Receive ownership of all that is good.
Woah!
Then in the Eden creation narrative there is a calling there as well.
The human is called to work (עבד ‘avad) and to keep (שמר shamar) the Garden in Eden.
These are words that will later describe the priests who work and keep the temple.
If only we had a kingdom of priests to represent God to the nations.
Melody Cycle 1 Choice
Genesis 2:16 - 3:24
The Choice portion of the melody starts with the divine command not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and bad.
However, between the divine command and the Fall, the authors insert an example of Yahweh seeing, taking, building, and giving in 2:18-22.
Unlike Yahweh, the humans see what is good in their eyes, then take, eat, and give non-life.
The inevitable consequences follow.
God acknowledges the unfortunate new state of His creation but makes some promises worth noting on the way out, see Genesis 3:15.
Melody Cycle 1 Division
Outside of Eden, future generations escalate the spiral of Division in the characteristic human cycle.
As predicted in Genesis 3:16, they conceive for themselves instead of receiving from God, then experience great anguish.
Cain kills Abel.
Lamech takes two wives and murders a boy for striking him.
The Sons of Elohim see and take the beautiful, tov, daughters of humanity in a parallel spiritual rebellion.
We end up with the Nephilim (the fallen ones), and the whole land is ruined by Genesis 6:12.
If Genesis 1 had been a singular creation event then the whole cosmos would have been a very short, rather pointless, project.
Fortunately for us, creation, life, and blessing are repeated notes in God's song.
Melody Cycle 1 Collapse
Genesis 6:13 - 7:24
The Collapse here is one we all know well.
God brings about a great leveling act to cleanse the land via the Flood.
This is a clear return to the Genesis 1:2 precreation state.
By the end of Genesis 7, the world is again in the same watery chaos image of nothing, minus one small difference… a boat, covered with atonement, preserving seed.
This symbol of God preserving life is of no small significance for you and me.
Noah, seven other people, and a whole bunch of animals sit and wait until Yahweh does it again.
“How long?
Oh LORD?” the poets say.
How long until You do it again?
Genesis 1-7: Pattern Breakers!
In the same way that Genesis 1-7 is the template for the characteristic humans, it is also the template for pattern breakers!
Clearly, Enoch and Noah don’t follow the characteristic division and collapse cycle.
Their patterns will be clear and discussed elsewhere, but the most commonly overlooked pattern breaker in this cycle is the delightful ski jump at the end of chapter 4.
There is a moment where the rapid division descent takes a sharp up turn.
Everyone reads the words, but we often overlook the significance of this pattern breaking moment.
From 4:1 to 4:24 we see characteristic human choices to establish “normal” human behavior.
In that section, Eve claims to have made a man all by herself in comparison to Yahweh.

The authors use clever wordplay by noting only that Cain was conceived, the same Hebrew root word as heron (הרנך) from 3:16, but with no mention of their male child being called a son, the Hebrew word ben (בן).
Cain, however, is invited by God to be a pattern breaker in the next generation.
He can rule over sin, but instead he too chooses the broad path of non-life.
Then Cain’s wife will also conceive, but again no mention of their child, a different Enoch, being a son.
We have already seen where that path spirals out of control in the division section above.
Let’s skip to verse 25, where we will see something new that you won’t find on the division spiral.
In the closing section of chapter 4, verses 25 and 26, we start with intentionally repeated words from verse 1, “Adam knew his wife again,” but things go differently this time!
First, right at this pivot, the Hebrew name for Adam changes from The Adam, i.e. “The Human”, to just Adam, a personal name.
Conversely, Eve’s name was used in verse 1, but now she called only “his wife” to emphasize their union over individuality.
Next, the authors hint that something is new by only stating that she bears a son (yalad ben) with no mention of her conceiving.
So it’s the same, but also opposite in every subtle way.
Interesting.
4:1 Now, the human knew his wife Eve,
and she conceived and she gave birth
4:25 and Adam knew his wife again
and she gave birth to a son,
To be clear, she did conceive for every birth.
She clearly became pregnant at some point, but the authors do not mention it, since this birth is not all about Eve.
Finally, Adam’s wife shows her new perspective by giving the glory to Elohim, not herself.
She sees life as a gift to be received instead of an act accomplished by herself.
Then it hits you... she is the first to break the pattern!
She was the first to take the fruit, but she was also the first to turn back and make a different choice.
We all fail, that’s really nothing new, but we don’t all turn back to God.
Eve, Mother of all living-ones, is famous for Genesis 3:6-7, but she was also the first to receive the fruit.
Welcome home!
I say “Welcome home” because Eden is a place where heaven and earth overlap.
A place where human and divine work together as one (yachad in Hebrew).
It has always been more than just a physical spot on the map.
Let's bring life to the next generation together!
Here are the pattern breaker choices in the first cycle of the melody, starting with Eve.
Genesis 4:25-26
4:25 and Adam (the personal name, not the characteristic Human) knew his wife again
and she gave birth to a son (yalad ben),
and she named him "Seth (שת)," because,
“God has appointed (שת) me another seed in place of Abel, for Cain killed him.”
26 and to Seth, to him also a son was born (yalad ben);
and he called his name Enosh.
then it was begun, to call on the name of Yahweh.
Eve and Seth are living out only the second half of Genesis 3:16, the necessary labor pains, instead of the greatly multiplied grief of conception that we saw in 4:1-24.

In your life too expect unavoidable labor pains as humans learn to be images of God, but do try to avoid the greatly multiplied grief that comes with conceiving your own plans over trusting God's word.
3:16 and to the woman he said,
[Part 1] "I will greatly multiply your grief and your conception (והרנך va- heron),
[Part 2] in grief you will birth children (yalad benim, sons),
If these phrases were used only in this verse, the mystery would be impossible to unravel, but that's not how the Bible works.
The authors slowly reveal additional information as stories repeat to invite hearers to become active participants.
For example, these subtle “conceive” verse “bear a son” word choices will echo not just in chapter four with Eve herself, but with other mothers in Scripture.
To conceive is not a 100% match for pending great anguish, but it’s a hint used more than a few times.
Consider: Avram and Hagar conceive with Ishmael, Genesis 16:4, but Avraham and Sarah conceive and bear a son with Isaac in Genesis 21:2.
David and Bathsheba initially conceive a child who died on the seventh day, 2 Samuel 11:5, but later bear a son, Solomon in 12:24-25.
The later stories inform the earlier Genesis 3:16 mystery.
As a teacher, I can identify this technique of putting an initial puzzle before students, a little mystery to figure out.
These authors have intentionally crafted a learning experience to find linked words that unlock a cryptic statement.
Focusing on ten words at a time doesn't work, you need the greater narrative.
Hum… a little riddle that requires time to unpack used for teaching… that sounds familiar... have you read the Sermon on the Mount recently?

Genesis 8-11: The Second Round of the Melody
Before we jump into the second cycle of the melody, I’d like to pause for a moment and congratulate you for making it to the center of the center of this guide.
We find ourselves in Genesis chapter 8, section 8 of this guide, and it feels symbolic, as if very early in the morning on the first day of a new week, the dawn of new creation.
It's Sunday morning!
We’re hopeful like the 8th son of Jesse.
Give us something new!
I sure hope something important happens! …
Sure enough, something truly remarkable and significant will happen.
Genesis 1 will replay in Genesis 8:1-9:18, but in new ways for a new generation.
A pattern is not a pattern unless it repeats.
So in Genesis 1-11, the introduction to the Bible, we see the cycle of life, not once, but twice.
The Hebrew Bible authors are quietly going to reshape the way you see the world.
The Spirit has breathed into them a truth that God never stops bringing creation, life, and blessing.
Let’s reflect on their words and try to become listeners that live out Psalm 1:1-1:3.
The cycle begins again in Genesis 8:1, unmistakably, right in the chiastic center of the flood narrative.
Life begins with the presence of God, shown again as Ruakh (רוח), the Hebrew word that means wind, breath, or presence.
Additionally, we introduce a new highly significant word, zakar, which means not just “remembered,” but more accurately “remembered and acted on it!”
8:1 “And Elohim remembered (zakar) Noah
and all the living creatures
and all the beasts that were with him in the ark;
and Elohim caused to pass
a Spirit/wind (Ruakh) to cover the land
and the waters subsided.”
To help you compare the two “about to act” creation moments, here is the precreation state of Genesis 1:2, where the Ruakh was over the face of the waters.
1:2 Now, the land was wild and waste (תהו ווהו • tohu va-vohu),
and darkness was over the face of the deep abyss (תהום • tehom),
but the breath (Ruakh) of Elohim was hovering over the face of the waters (המים)
This guide is not a deep dive on the Holy Spirit, the third person of the Trinity, for that consider a work like Tyler Staton’s The Familiar Stranger or the Spirit of God collection.
However, I do want to at least point out that the Spirit did not come only after Jesus' death at Pentecost in Acts 2.
The same Spirit has been present and active since page one, doing what God does best, breathing life into His creation.
Genesis always begins with the personal presence of God, and the biblical authors help us understand that simple truth by mentioning His Ruakh.
By the way, props to Stephen Langton, the 1205 AD Archbishop of Canterbury, who did the Bible chapter divisions that we still use today.
He intentionally/accidentally chose to put the first melody into exactly seven chapters.
His chapter breaks aren’t perfect.
He did the best he could with the Latin Vulgate and he only did it to ease citation, not structure the text, but this one was a winner: exactly seven chapters to complete the first melody.
Bible scholars love to point out happy coincidences, see Matthew 1-4.
Next, Elohim commands Noah and his family to go out from the ark, blessing them Genesis 1 style:
9:1 And Elohim blessed Noah and his sons and he said to them,
“Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the land.
All is good in blissful creation at the top of the mountain with God.
However, it makes an informed reader wonder what will come next… and worry.
The authors continue the Creation, Choice, Division of Relationships, and Collapse cycle using very clear notes.
In the second pass through the melody, Genesis 8-11, notice that the authors never replay a story identically.
Each cycle fills out the one before, quietly expanding your sense of what each note is communicating.
By the end of only two laps, you’ll reflect back on Genesis 1-7 in ways that you couldn’t see before.
Melody Cycle 2 Creation
Genesis 8:1-9:18
We again hear Creation notes of blessing, but with a new twist, the humans and animals are partnering with God in the creation process.
In Genesis 1:27 when Elohim created the ‘Image of God,’, the authors used the phrase “male and female” he created them.
That phrase in Hebrew is za-KAR oonKAY vah (זָכָ֥ר וּנְקֵבָ֖ה) and it became a creation note that we should listen for.
In this new creation story, Noah is bringing out the animals who were put into the ark za-KAR oonKAY vah, male and female.
The repeated words are creation vocabulary that the authors didn't want you to miss.
In fact they repeat the phrase four times when the animals board the boat, za-KAR oonKay vah.
By the way, we are stepping around the rabbit hole where the letters for zakar, זכר, mean both “male child” from this phrase AND zakar זכר, “remembered,” in Genesis 8:1, too many hyperlinks!
But a listener in Hebrew would certainly hear the zakar creation notes.
These new creation events continue in blissful harmony with a sacrifice, covenant, and a sign of the covenant, the rainbow.
What could go wrong?
However, we know the cycle will repeat since Genesis 8:21 warns us that the human heart has not changed.
Melody Cycle 2 Calling
Genesis 7:1-5 and 8:15-17
7:1 “Go, you and all your household, into the ark
for you I have seen as a righteous one before me in this generation… to keep alive seed on the face of the land.”
8:15 And Elohim spoke to Noah, saying, “Go out from the ark, you and your wife and your sons and your sons’ wives with you.

From every living thing with you from all flesh, birds and animals and every creeper that creeps on the land, make them go out with you, so they can swarm in the land and be fruitful and multiply in the land.”
Melody Cycle 2 Choice
Genesis 9:19-29
The next generation repeats the sins of the old as the Choice notes begin to play in the new Eden space.
Noah takes the wine in an illicit way by getting drunk.
Then he uncovers himself in the middle of his tent.
These are verbal echoes of Adam and Eve taking the fruit in the middle of the garden, then realizing they were naked.
Finally, Ham “saw the nakedness of his father”.
In Hebrew, a man's nakedness is his wife, Leviticus 18:7-8 spells this out plainly.
The act is so terrible that the authors use a common Hebrew euphemism.

Despite our modern debates and mystery, “seeing the nakedness” is a standard phrase stating that Ham had sex with his father’s wife (if you would like to have more evidence go read Ezekiel 22:10 in a literal translation).
The word choice ties this unthinkable moment into the “seeing what is good in his eyes” theme.
Translators face an impossible task here.
They need to maintain the “seeing” hyperlink, discern the idioms, and keep it to five words or less.

So they usually just follow the pattern of prior translations, throw their hands in the air, and give a literal word-for-word translation, leaving interpretation to the reader (which is fine, let commentaries explain it).
Next, much like God did in the Garden exit, this new state results in Noah giving blessings to Yahweh the Elohim of Shem and curses to Canaan.
Wait, Canaan?
Where did Ham go?
Canaan, the father of the Canaanites, was Ham’s fourth and final son, but the authors don’t explain the generational jump at all.
Instead, you are forced to use your imagination to fill in the gap.
Melody Cycle 2 Division
Genesis 9:22-11:5
It is no surprise that Division comes next.
In fact, it has already begun.
Ham’s horrific power play fractured the family, causing the three brothers to divide into the nations.
The spiral continues with Nimrod building Babylon, the icon for communal evil choices used throughout the Bible.
Finally, Yahweh does a thorough investigation of the situation in Genesis 11:5, “And Yahweh came down to see the city and the tower that the sons of humanity built.”
Dangerous notes are beginning to play.
Melody Cycle 2 Collapse
Genesis 11:7-9
In this cycle, the collapse is Yahweh scattering the civilization of Babylon at the Tower of Babel.
11:9 “from there Yahweh scattered them upon the face of all the land.”
In our generation, scattering a nation doesn't carry the same weight, but in this context, these are Collapse notes.
For example, in 9:19, the authors describe the “scattering” using the Hebrew word naphats, which Psalm 2:9 uses to “shatter” like a pot.
So God shattered the people of Babylon like a pot onto the face of the land.
God has initiated the collapse in both cycles so far to set the stage for new life, but that will not always be the case as the melody continues.
With only two passes through the melody, we can already hear many distinctive notes that emerge from the Genesis 1-11 characteristic human cycle.
Here are only a few:

Genesis 8-11: Pattern Breakers!
Who are the pattern breakers in the second round of the melody and how will God preserve life through them?
It is a shorter melody, so there are fewer pattern breakers, but we still see a few.
We have primarily one man, Noah and the ark, who passed through the first archetypal flood collapse.
He was called and received the calling.
He listens and obeys.
Super fun side quest, look for how other people are called in the Bible to start a new genesis!

Consider moments like Moses being called to rise up and cross the Reed Sea, Samuel to arise and anoint David, Joseph to get up and flee to Egypt (Matthew 2), so Jesus could fulfill being called out of Egypt (disorder).
That's a great note to track!
You will come to realize it’s true even today.
God blesses and calls us out of chaos, SO THAT we can be a blessing to others.
Anyway…
In the new creation Noah builds an altar and makes a going-up offering to Yahweh.
Yahweh smells the soothing smell and responds in blessing.
This sacrifice note is mirrored in other rounds of the melody in creative ways, but we are trying to stay focused.
The next pattern breakers are Shem and Japheth.
They do the opposite of Ham and cover their father’s nakedness.
This time, not seeing their father's nakedness is simple and literal.
These authors use clever wordplay even when the subject matter makes us feel uncomfortable.
Subtle symmetries, through repeated words, help readers see the inversion.
Afterwards, Noah blesses Yahweh the Elohim of Shem and again a remnant is preserved through Shem’s line.
Genesis 11:10-26 gives another ten-generation bridge, mirroring chapter 5.
It is the tenth, Avram, who will partner with God to start the next melody cycle.
Will Avram be the one who will crush the head of the snake?
Genesis 11:27-22:19: Cycles Three to Seven with Avraham
With Genesis 1-11 complete, we come to the next major section of Genesis and start the third cycle of the melody.
It opens with a title in Genesis 11:27, “Now these are the generations of Terakh.”
Then, following the Genesis 1 pattern, we have a new precreation state in 11:28-32.
This time, the symbols for non-life are not watery chaos or a dry desert.
Instead, if you read with eyes looking for symbols of death and disorder, you will notice:
And Haran died before his father Terakh
And Sarai was barren, she had no child
And they went out … to go to the land of Canaan; and they went as far as Haran
And Terakh died in Haran
Without God’s presence, the “wild and waste” from Genesis 1:2 is depicted with these new symbols of precreation non-life.
These authors are very clever and give us a small cairn in the word Haran that we are on the right track.
The Genesis 3:16 word to conceive heron הרן, sounds a lot like these new symbols of death: Haran the brother (הרן) has the very same letters, and Haran the place (חרן) is only one letter off.

Most of our English translations even spell those two words identically to show they are connected, but none are able to show the Hebrew wordplay connection to Genesis 3:16 properly (these authors are amazing).
Genesis 12:1 then starts the creation section of melody three with Yahweh speaking to Avram (the new ruakh), who steps into the role of Adam and Noah.
In this generation, he will partner with God to once again bring about creation, life, and blessing.
The ruakh and the calling come together.
12:1 “And Yahweh said to Avram,
Get yourself going…”
It’s a wonderful and significant speech, but a bit long for this guide.
Go read it!
It calls Avram to come out, much like Noah was called out of the Ark.
The calling here is crisp and clean, perhaps Avram will crush the head of the snake and just help us all avoid the collapse?
Perhaps not.
Well, at least like Noah he will receive his calling and pass through the collapse without failure?
Perhaps not there as well.
People are complex and the melody is growing in complexity with us.
We’ll be tracking the ups and downs with Abraham through five melody cycles.
In this cycle, Yahweh kickstarts genesis with a call to Avram and expands the new Creation promise, stating: “in you all the families of the land will find blessing”.
Verses 4 and 5 then tell another journey story, but now with God present.
Interestingly, this second journey was perhaps the same trip, see Acts 7:2.
This reminds me of Genesis 1:2 where darkness was over the face of the tehom, the waters of death, but the Spirit of Elohim was hovering over the face of the waters.
Those might be the same physical states, just described first without God's presence and then with it.
The difference is not what you would see with your eyes.
The difference is God.
Next, Avram journeys throughout the land with Yahweh in Genesis 12:6-9, much like Adam and Eve walked with God in the windy part of the day.
An informed reader enjoys the bliss of Creation notes, but is again worried about what will happen next.
Yahweh makes a clear, unconditioned declaration in Genesis 12:7: “To your seed I will give this land.”
Will Avram trust and obey, staying in the land that Yahweh has promised?
You already know.
You have been shaped by the melody without even realizing it.
The cycle will continue as long as the human heart is unchanged, but God will continue to preserve life through it all.
The One who IS does not change.

We could continue discussing the melody with the choice in Egypt of seeing, taking, and giving, then a division of relationships with the “brothers,” Avram and his nephew Lot, followed by a collapse of four kings sweeping away five.
Instead of continuing through the cycle in a linear way from this point, which is already getting pretty lengthy, let’s mention only the collapse moments that mark the seven cycles of Genesis 1-22.
Working through each full cycle with your own group is worth your time.
The story takes a much closer look at one person and we see the complexity of humans as we are pattern breakers one moment, then go right back to being characteristic ten seconds later.
The creative twists will be surprising and rewarding as you meditate on the melody.
The seven collapse stories of Genesis 1-22 are:
Melody Cycle 1 Collapse
Genesis 7:17-24

The Flood: 7:23 And he wiped away every standing-thing that was upon the face of the land, from humanity to animals to creepers and to birds of the skies, and they were wiped away from the land; and only Noah was left remaining, and those with him in the ark.
Melody Cycle 2 Collapse
Genesis 11:8-9
The Scattering: 11:8-9 And Yahweh scattered them from there upon the face of all the land, and they stopped building the city.
Therefore, its name was called Babylon (Babel), because there Yahweh made-babble of the language of all the land, and from there Yahweh scattered them upon the face of all the land.
Melody Cycle 3 Collapse
Genesis 14:1-12
Sodom #1: Four kings from Mesopotamia waged war against five kings, which included the people, possessions, and food of Sodom and Gomorrah.
Avram’s nephew Lot is taken in the process.
This is our first collapse of human origin, but the flood language remains the same as they sweep away.
Meanwhile, Avram is symbolically in the ark, but then goes out with 318 men and “God’s help” to restore life.
Melody Cycle 4 Collapse
Genesis 16:6
Hagar #1: This melody ends with a rape victim, pregnant, fleeing in the wilderness with nowhere to go and no human that loves her in the world.
Only Yahweh sees this Egyptian slave-girl.
From Yahweh’s perspective the world has come to an end again, except for this time, it’s in the life of only 1 person.
In this fourth cycle of the melody the Choice, Division of Relationships, and Collapse happen in only six verses in 16:1-6.
It’s an explosion where these authors can replay the whole story with very few words once you know the notes to listen for.
A single choice by Sarai and Avram to take their Egyptian slave-girl Hagar causes a violent division of every relationship leading to a very sudden collapse.
God, however, enters our mess, sees Hagar in the wilderness, and restores life in ways that feel interestingly compromised, making the best of a broken situation.
Read this in-depth Hagar article for more insights.
Melody Cycle 5 Collapse
Genesis 19:15-29
Sodom #2: 19:24 and Yahweh caused it to rain over Sodom and over Gomorrah, sulphur and fire from Yahweh from the skies.
The notes of this culminating collapse can’t be missed as it uses a flood of words to connect the melodies.
Noteworthy in this story is that Lot and his family are saved due to Yahweh’s mercy, 19:16, and the phrase “Yahweh remembered (zakar) Avraham" is used in 19:29, when Avraham wasn’t even there.
These authors don’t use words for no reason.
Melody Cycle 6 Collapse
Genesis 21:14-16
Hagar #2: The sixth melody cycle again ends in a collapse, but when you look at the details with your group, hopefully you notice something odd, a new twist in the melody.
Abraham and Sarah are blessed with Isaac, a divine command is given to listen to the voice of your wife, and the divine command is followed perfectly.
We see abiding obedience showing love for God as John would put it.
Great!
Doesn't Proverbs tell us that now all things will work out well?
There is so much here to unpack and you absolutely must compare both times Abraham listens to the voice of his wife.
There is subtlety and complexity to this message.
I’ll just say that the result of passing the test with Hagar is a collapse.
Wait what?
In this world, obedience can result in suffering and yield a collapse.
Store that idea away.
This is a Job moment not a Proverbs moment.
Hagar is sent into the wilderness with Ishmael, her, most likely, 17 year old boy lad, the Hebrew word na’ar.
She is a slave-girl no longer and has her son with her, but the water runs dry and death seems inevitable.
Does this remind you of Genesis 2:5, a lifeless desert with no water?
But Elohim listens to the voice of the na’ar (a fun wordplay on the meaning of Ishmael’s name), converting Collapse into Creation once more.
The turning point is a messenger of Elohim calling to Hagar from the skies.
Hagar is told not to be afraid, but to ‘get up’ and take the lad with her hand.
Elohim will make him into a great nation.
Sound familiar?
The same promise was given to Avram.
Elohim opened her eyes and she saw a well of water at Beer Sheva, the Well of Seven.
She fills the water skin and she gives life to the lad as well.
Not a single word is unimportant as Hagar, the non-chosen, becomes an unexpected partner in creation, life, and blessing.
Melody Cycle 7 Collapse
Genesis 22:1-10
The Binding of Isaac: The seventh collapse is told one syllable at a time as Avraham sends out his hand and takes the eater, the knife, to slay his son.

This collapse is brought about by God’s command, the calling of Abraham again with the words “Get yourself going…” (lekh lekha) precisely mirroring the initial calling of Avram, and Abraham’s perfect obedience.
Hyperlinking all the way back to the start of his journey hints that everything in between has been leading up to this moment and Abraham is no longer just 75% ready to listen.
Avraham's struggle to trust God is put to the ultimate test and Abraham is all in, but God’s song is again at the precipice of non-life as the promised seed is bound on the altar.
When we open the pages to this collapse, we find quite a bit more than just a flood.
The seventh collapse necessitates a more in-depth discussion to make sure we all see a bit more of what the authors are communicating.
The Melody Points to Jesus
Without really planning it, we’ll carefully study the seventh melody and something will happen where the story naturally turns to Jesus.
Let’s ride the wave together.
The Seventh Collapse: Avraham’s Test
As you might have suspected, the seventh collapse of the melody and the creation moment after are rather significant.
Without even knowing the rest of the story, a careful reader of the Hebrew Bible would know that when this melody repeats, it will reveal God in a major way.
Indeed, the concept of the Melody and the Test are both HUGE topics on their own, but they are so interwoven that we have no choice but to jump into Genesis 22:1-19 with both feet!

The collapse opens with a clear title in 22:1 stating that Avraham is tested.
When you think “test,” try to imagine an experience that reveals the truth, not a stressful exam with right and wrong answers.
It reveals what is already present through action.
For example, Noah was called righteous in 6:9 by the narrator, but he still had to actually build the Ark in 6:22 and Yahweh sees the truth in 7:1.
Likewise, Avraham was called righteous in 15:6, but he would still have to go through his test in Genesis 22.
God is giving him a quest to reveal truth, not tempting him to do evil.
There is a difference.
God is asking him to trust in His wisdom beyond anything he can see with his eyes.
It is clearly not a test God would give you or me, but the test fits the man if you reflect on Avraham’s whole story.
Jesus illustrated that tests are specific to the person when he spoke to the rich young ruler.
That man’s test was based on the thing that separated him from God, his wealth.
He needed to trust God and give away all he had to the poor, then follow Jesus.
In his case, it only revealed his inability to take a radical step of trust, and he went away downcast.
When God chose “Father Abraham” to initiate His restoration plan, he knew exactly what test would reveal him and he knew that Avraham would trust his voice.
In the same way, The Father knew what test would reveal The Son and he trusted the Son to complete it.
That test reveals God to us.
Consider Psalm 22:31 and John 3:16.
The hyperlinks from Genesis 22 to Jesus are impossible to miss.
It is a test for both the father and the son.
However, they traveled together perfectly aligned, both before and after all the details are known.
The phrase “and the two of them went, together-as-one” (yachad in Hebrew) is repeated three times.
Isaac put the wood on his back and walked with his father at the same physical place where Jesus will later be lifted up on the cross.
Keep in mind that all of this was written hundreds of years before Jesus ever walked the earth.
That’s worth a long walk and a cup of tea.
Finally, Avraham’s collapse and Jesus' collapse end the same way, the son is returned to life.
Avraham is revealed.
Elohim sees.
And a going-up offering of a ram substitutes for Avraham’s offspring.
As always, God makes sure that creation, life, and blessing have the final say over a collapse.
Before we leave this story, let’s consider what it might have meant to Jesus.
What thoughts raced through Jesus’ head as he mentally recounted this story in the Garden of Gethsemane?
And when did He fully grasp the details?
John the Baptist publicly named Jesus as the “Lamb of God” in John 1:29.
I think Jesus knew fully what that meant.
Yahweh’s character has been known since Exodus 34:6-7, but Jesus would still have to go through the test.
This plan, made before time began, is how God would reveal who He is to us.
God loves you.
He has said it in His Word, and He has shown it in His actions.
He has passed the test to show that nothing will separate Him from joining us even when he knows it’s coming.
Then the outpouring of blessings given by God’s oath “on the heel” of the test is worth reading a few times.
Genesis 22:16-18, Yahweh’s Oath (שבע sheva) at the conclusion of melody seven (שבע sheva):
22:16 “I swear an oath (שבע sheva) by myself, utterance of Yahweh,
on account of the fact that you did this thing,
and you did not withhold your son, your only one,
17 that I will certainly bless you,
and I will certainly multiply your seed,
like the stars of the skies,
and like the sand upon the edge of the sea,
and your seed will inherit the gate of their enemies,
18 and all the nations of the land will find blessing in your seed,
on the heel of the fact that you listened to my voice.”
Let’s read it again, “all nations will find blessing in your seed.”
The author wants you to remember Genesis 3:15 by mentioning the words “heel” and the future “seed” so close together.
Two words are more than enough to see this connection.
3:15 And I will set hostility
between you and the woman,
and between your seed and her seed,
he will strike your head
and you will strike his heel."
However, the people would have to wait a long time until God repeats these specific notes.
The Genesis Melody won't fail, but it does require waiting patiently for God’s teleios timing.
Seeing the Melody in the New Testament
The Genesis Melody is about a time when God sees (or sometimes causes) a collapse and instead of it being the end, it is an opportunity to bring about a new creation, a genesis.
We’ll briefly pause our review of Genesis and consider The Genesis Melody as it plays out in the Gospel According to Luke.
You hopefully know this cycle of the melody well.
Jesus, being the monogenes (μονογενής), is utterly unique, but, sure enough, He fulfills the same melody pattern.
In Luke, the story opens with God’s Spirit creating life in two impossible places of non-life: a barren womb long past childbearing and one that had never known a man.
Luke starts, not just with the birth of Jesus to the virgin Mary, but with the interwoven story of John the Baptist’s birth to Zechariah and Elizabeth.
The author of this story saw that even the names of the parents were significant:
Zechariah, from the Hebrew Zakar-Yah זכריה, means “Yahweh Remembered, zakar.”
It's that zakar word again, the one that means “acts on his promise.”
Compare that with Genesis 8:1, “Elohim remembered, zakar, Noah” or 19:29, “Yahweh remembered, zakar, Avraham.”
Elizabeth, from the Hebrew Eli-Sheva אלישבע, means “My Elohim’s Oath”.
It’s that sheva, oath, word again!
Compare that with 22:16, “I swear an oath (שבע sheva).”
Zechariah and Elizabeth are set up as clear mirrors of Avraham and Sarah, childless at a good old age.
And if you put their names together, you literally have “Yahweh Remembered His Oath from Genesis 22!”
OK, I admit, I added that last bit, but “Zechariah Elizabeth” means that Yahweh made good, delivered on, remembered his oath to Abraham in Jesus and John was the forerunner of that good news.
The authors who handed over source material to the gentile Luke, see Luke 1:1, saw the Genesis melody at work.
They partnered with Luke to share the Good News about Jesus to all the nations via the same creation notes that echo Genesis, now appearing in Luke, chapters 1 and 2.
Jesus is then clearly called (identified) at John’s Baptism.
Luke’s story then has a choice in the wilderness for forty days and a matching test in Gethsemane before the end.
There is a journey with Jesus, just like Avram's journey with Yahweh.
Jesus and the Father are fully aligned, fully unified, completely faithful, the only ever, perfect Image of God.
However, in his generation there was still a division with the leaders of Israel (that’s putting it lightly).
Then a replay of the seventh cycle collapse at the cross.
Finally, this is the most important part, what comes after a collapse?
The author of life allows His own body, His Son, to experience collapse, from which God will…
You know exactly what happened next, on the third day no less, see Genesis 22:4.
The Genesis Melody has been written in Scripture for a thousand years.
Jesus surely said many similar things on the road to Emmaus in Luke 24, as he “opened the Scriptures” to his disciples.

The eighth melody cycle, 22:20-25:18, ends with Avraham's death and the scattering of his various sons.

Extra Sheva Observations

To bring this discussion full circle, let’s return to Genesis 21-22 once more to see evidence that these authors, with the help of the Spirit, already realized the significance of this forward pointing message.
Throughout Scripture the authors regularly highlight the most important concept of a literary unit by using key repeated words, known as lead words.
In this seventh cycle of the melody, which goes from the voice in the sky bringing life to Hagar and Ishmael, through the binding of Isaac, the primary lead word is clearly sheva.
The same Hebrew letters of sheva, שבע, form multiple Hebrew words.
Think of it like the English letters lead, which has multiple meanings: lead the way, pencil lead, or leader.
The Hebrew word sheva, שבע, means seven, oath, and, later, completion, making it a very significant word.
Perhaps you've noticed the number 7 gets used a lot.
The repeated use of sheva in this melody cycle is another cairn left by the authors to reinforce that we are on the right track.
It gives us confidence that we are indeed seeing the path that these authors laid out for us.
The sheva theme is everywhere in this melody cycle.
The creation notes open with Hagar and Ishmael at Beer-Sheva, the Well of Seven.
The middle section with Avimelek takes place at Beer-Sheva, centered on an oath, a sheva.
Then, after the mountain in Moriah, the literary unit ends with Avraham dwelling in Beer-Sheva.
The start, middle, and end are all at Beer-Sheva.
Everything points to Yahweh's culminating sheva, His oath.
In addition to the location, there are more sheva words used in Genesis 21-22 than you might guess.
The numbers tell the story:
In fact if you focus on only the use of sheva words in cycles three to seven with Avraham it becomes clear that the authors have intentionally marked this round of the melody as the Sheva Cycle.
By modern writing standards, the repeated use of sheva borders on excessive, but that’s exactly the point.
Listeners would hear the word as prominent and realize this is the seven-oath for completion.
Imagine sitting in the temple courts on Shabbat listening to Simeon read this text.

The word sheva appears nine times as this cycle builds toward the collapse, and then the 10th is Yahweh’s Sheva, His oath, the very first words of the new creation (plus two more Beer-Sheva uses to finish the literary unit).
Did ancient readers like Simeon emphasize the word each time for his hearers?
Let’s look at one example from Genesis 21:28-32, a “seemingly” insignificant passage.
The authors use extra sheva, שבע, words surrounding being a witness.
That’ll preach!
In this passage with Avraham and Avimelek, two men whose names mean Father of Nations and My Father is King, make the first human-to-human covenant in the Bible.
They mend the division cycle without directly mentioning God using a covenant.
That's interesting!

The testing and the collapse are still coming in Genesis 22, Abraham has made a lifetime of choices that need resolution, but we see a glimmer of hope in chapter 21 about how to slow down this crazy hamster wheel… covenant relationships with fellow images of God.
Covenants aren't as good as changed hearts, but usually it's the best option we have available outside of Eden.
Every generation has to renew a covenant, Isaac and Avimelek in Genesis 26, Jacob and Lavan in Genesis 31, and on into today.
This seventh cycle is packed with insights!
I’ll let you be the judge.
Do you agree that these authors intentionally marked the seventh cycle of the melody?
Did they count melodies from the beginning and intentionally work with the Spirit to reveal God to you?
How did they know, even then, to write the text in this way?

The seventh, culminating, oath cycle about fulfillment points to Jesus.
It is the highly structured Word of God given to us by humans working with the Ruakh of Elohim after all.

Your Next Steps
God's not finished and we’re not done.
Let's talk about next steps.

Read directly from God what the Spirit has breathed.
